claims.text: The initially single-phase high-entropy alloy can be CoCrFeMnNi with an FCC structure.
Nanoscale chemical fluctuations govern the emergence of brittle behavior by causing grain-boundary decohesion.
High-strain-rate shear at 10^-2 s^-1 and 1173 K can trigger chemical fluctuations and grain-boundary decohesion in the initially FCC high-entropy alloy.
A strain rate of 10^-2 s^-1 at 1173 K is a high-rate elevated-temperature deformation condition.
An ultra-high-vacuum environment mitigates oxidation and mixed metal-oxide film formation.
Dynamic amorphization is triggered by high-strain-rate shear in the proposed alloy and conditions.
Dynamic amorphization leads to grain-boundary decohesion.
Inverse Hall–Petch behavior leads to grain-boundary decohesion.
Grain-boundary decohesion decreases toughness and increases brittleness.
The specified treatment will decrease toughness by 20% relative to the initial baseline.
The initial alloy has a toughness of 100 MPa·m^1/2.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing otherwise controlled specimens with and without nanoscale chemical fluctuations under the specified deformation conditions.
Toughness, grain-boundary decohesion, and nanoscale chemical fluctuations are the proposed measured variables.
Failure to observe at least a 15% toughness decrease relative to baseline under the specified conditions falsifies the hypothesis.
The relationship between nanoscale chemical fluctuations and grain-boundary decohesion is not fully understood.
The roles of impurities and defects in the proposed behavior are not well established.

contradictions.description: Grain-boundary decohesion is labeled as the structural mediator, but the mechanism field also treats it as a downstream result of dynamic amorphization and inverse Hall–Petch behavior, making the proposed causal ordering circular or ambiguous.
